heading: Cold open
narration: Chipmakers publish lists of bugs in chips they have already shipped. Those lists exist because of how the work is done.

heading: Cold open
narration: Microchips are designed mostly as text: engineers describe a chip's behaviour in a hardware description language such as Verilog or VHDL, and software tools translate that description into logic gates and then into the geometric layout of billions of transistors.

heading: Cold open
narration: Both languages are IEEE standards. Most effort goes into proving the design before manufacture, through simulation, formal proofs and the foundry's rules.

heading: Cold open
narration: Those checks reduce risk, and the errata show they cannot remove it.

narration: Start with the language, because that is where the design actually lives.

heading: A chip begins as a description of what it does
narration: A hardware description language looks like code, and engineers type it in an editor like any programmer.

heading: A chip begins as a description of what it does
narration: It describes structure and behaviour that exist all at once: these signals connect here, this value updates on every tick of the clock, this block waits for that one.

heading: A chip begins as a description of what it does
narration: The two dominant languages, Verilog and VHDL, along with an extended form called SystemVerilog, are published as standards by the IEEE.

args.meaning: text that describes structure and behaviour that exist all at once

heading: A chip begins as a description of what it does
narration: That is how every tool vendor and every design team can agree on what a given line of text means.

heading: A chip begins as a description of what it does
narration: The agreement is not a detail. Without a shared, written definition of the language, a design could mean one thing in the simulator and something slightly different in the tool that builds it.

args.meaning: text that describes structure and behaviour that exist all at once
args.boundary: it does not describe steps to be run one after another

heading: A chip begins as a description of what it does
narration: Most designs are written at what engineers call the register-transfer level. A register is a small store that holds a value.

heading: A chip begins as a description of what it does
narration: The description says how values move between registers, and what logic transforms them on the way, at each edge of the clock.

heading: A chip begins as a description of what it does
narration: Nothing at this level says where a transistor sits or how long a wire is.

heading: A chip begins as a description of what it does
narration: That separation is deliberate. It lets a team reason about what the chip should compute before anyone decides what it physically looks like, and it lets the same description be rebuilt for a different factory later.

heading: Synthesis turns the description into gates the factory already knows how to make
narration: The next step is called logic synthesis, and it is done by software.

heading: Synthesis turns the description into gates the factory already knows how to make
narration: The synthesis tool reads the register-transfer description and maps it onto a library of standard cells.

heading: Synthesis turns the description into gates the factory already knows how to make
narration: A standard cell is a small, pre-designed circuit — a gate that performs AND, a gate that inverts a signal, a storage element called a flip-flop — drawn and characterised in advance for one specific manufacturing process.

heading: Synthesis turns the description into gates the factory already knows how to make
narration: The factory, usually called a foundry, or a library vendor working with it, has measured how fast each cell switches and how much power it draws under different conditions of voltage and temperature.

heading: Synthesis turns the description into gates the factory already knows how to make
narration: The output of synthesis is a netlist: a list of cells and the wires that connect them.

heading: Synthesis turns the description into gates the factory already knows how to make
narration: Here is the first place the "how we know" question bites. Synthesis does not simply translate; it optimises, rewriting logic to be smaller or faster.

heading: Synthesis turns the description into gates the factory already knows how to make
narration: So the netlist is not a line-by-line copy of what the engineer wrote.

heading: Synthesis turns the description into gates the factory already knows how to make
narration: To confirm the two still mean the same thing, teams run equivalence checking, a formal method that proves mathematically that the netlist and the original description produce identical outputs for every input.

heading: Synthesis turns the description into gates the factory already knows how to make
narration: It is not a test that tries examples. It is a proof for every input, and that difference matters for everything that follows.

heading: Producer POV
narration: Deep-sea science builds conclusions from incomplete observations, damaged specimens, sonar, water samples and tiny windows of footage.

heading: Verification samples behaviour, then proves what it can
narration: That question, asked about animals, is exactly the right one to ask about chips.

heading: Verification samples behaviour, then proves what it can
narration: A modern processor has far more possible internal states than any simulation could ever visit.

heading: Verification samples behaviour, then proves what it can
narration: So no one observes a chip's behaviour exhaustively. Verification engineers build a testbench, a surrounding program that feeds the design inputs and checks its outputs against a reference model of what should happen.

heading: Verification samples behaviour, then proves what it can
narration: On many teams verification takes more effort than writing the design itself, though published estimates of the split vary and this script will not quote one.

heading: Verification samples behaviour, then proves what it can
narration: Engineers generate constrained random stimulus, enormous numbers of plausible but unplanned input sequences, because bugs hide in combinations no one thought to write by hand.

heading: Verification samples behaviour, then proves what it can
narration: Then they measure coverage: which lines executed, which states were reached, which scenarios the plan said must occur.

heading: Verification samples behaviour, then proves what it can
narration: Coverage is the honest part. It tells the team what was exercised and, by subtraction, what was not.

heading: Verification samples behaviour, then proves what it can
narration: Where simulation cannot reach, formal verification steps in. A tool is given a property — this buffer never overflows, these two requests are never granted at once — and searches for any sequence of inputs that breaks it.

heading: Verification samples behaviour, then proves what it can
narration: If none exists, the property is proven within the bounds the tool was given.

args.title: Verification
args.note: each method covers a gap the others leave

heading: Verification samples behaviour, then proves what it can
narration: For large designs, teams also load the description onto emulation hardware, or onto reconfigurable chips called FPGAs, which run the logic far faster than simulation and let real software boot on a design that does not physically exist yet. Each method covers a gap the others leave.

heading: Physical design turns a list of gates into geometry
narration: Only now does the chip acquire a shape. Physical design begins with floorplanning: deciding where large blocks such as memories and processor cores will sit, and how power reaches them.

heading: Physical design turns a list of gates into geometry
narration: Placement software then positions every standard cell from the netlist. Clock tree synthesis builds the network that delivers the clock signal so that it arrives at every flip-flop at nearly the same moment.

heading: Physical design turns a list of gates into geometry
narration: Routing draws the metal wires that connect everything, stacked in many layers above the transistors.

heading: Physical design turns a list of gates into geometry
narration: All of this is automated, because the number of cells is far too large for hands, but engineers steer it constantly, adjusting constraints and re-running when results fall short.

heading: Physical design turns a list of gates into geometry
narration: How do they know when results fall short? Mainly through static timing analysis.

heading: Physical design turns a list of gates into geometry
narration: Instead of simulating signals, the tool adds up the delay along every path between registers, using the characterised cell data and estimates of wire delay, and checks that each signal arrives before the next clock edge.

heading: Physical design turns a list of gates into geometry
narration: A path that is too slow is called a timing violation. Static timing analysis is powerful because it is exhaustive over paths without needing any input patterns.

args.meaning: adds up the delay along every path between registers
args.boundary: only as good as the delay models it is fed

heading: Physical design turns a list of gates into geometry
narration: Its boundary is that it is only as good as the delay models it is fed, which is why the careful measurement work done by the foundry matters so much.

heading: Signoff checks the layout against the factory's own rules
narration: Before a design leaves the team, it goes through signoff. Design rule checking compares every shape in the layout against the foundry's rule set: minimum widths, minimum spacings, how layers may overlap.

heading: Signoff checks the layout against the factory's own rules
narration: Those rules encode what the manufacturing process can reliably print. Layout versus schematic checking extracts the circuit that the geometry actually forms and confirms it matches the netlist.

heading: Signoff checks the layout against the factory's own rules
narration: Parasitic extraction calculates the resistance and capacitance of the real wires, and timing is checked again with those values.

heading: Signoff checks the layout against the factory's own rules
narration: A design that passes all of this is handed off in a step still called tape-out, a name commonly traced to the era when layouts were shipped on magnetic tape.

heading: Signoff checks the layout against the factory's own rules
narration: The layout becomes a set of photomasks, the stencils used to pattern each layer of the wafer.

heading: Signoff checks the layout against the factory's own rules
narration: Here the design world meets the public standards bodies. SEMI, the industry association for semiconductor manufacturing, publishes the SEMI International Standards used across equipment, materials and masks, so that a design from one company can be built with tools from many others.

heading: Signoff checks the layout against the factory's own rules
narration: NIST, the United States national measurement institute, works on semiconductor metrology — how to measure features far too small to see, and how sure anyone can be of that measurement.

heading: Signoff checks the layout against the factory's own rules
narration: These bodies do not design chips. They supply the shared definitions and measurements that let a design be trusted outside the room it was made in.

heading: The first chips back from the factory are the real experiment
narration: Everything up to tape-out is prediction. The first wafers back from the foundry are where prediction meets matter.

heading: The first chips back from the factory are the real experiment
narration: Engineers run bring-up: they power the first chips, check that clocks start, load test software, and compare behaviour against the models.

heading: The first chips back from the factory are the real experiment
narration: To make this possible, designers add circuitry whose only purpose is to be tested.

heading: The first chips back from the factory are the real experiment
narration: Scan chains link the flip-flops so their contents can be shifted out and read, which lets automated test equipment check each manufactured chip for physical defects.

heading: The first chips back from the factory are the real experiment
narration: This practice is called design for test, and it is why a chip can be checked after manufacture, not only before.

heading: The first chips back from the factory are the real experiment
narration: When bring-up finds a bug that slipped through, the outcome depends on where it lives.

heading: The first chips back from the factory are the real experiment
narration: Some bugs can be worked around in software or firmware. Others require a respin: corrected masks and another trip through the factory, which costs time and money.

heading: The first chips back from the factory are the real experiment
narration: Manufacturers also publish lists of known bugs in shipped products, usually called errata.

heading: The first chips back from the factory are the real experiment
narration: Those documents are some of the most candid public evidence about chip design, because they show directly that verification reduces risk without removing it.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: In the edit, watch for the shift between two kinds of evidence.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Some steps, like equivalence checking, formal proofs and static timing analysis, are exhaustive within a stated model.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Others, like simulation and bring-up, are samples. The animation draws those differently.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: A proven claim is drawn solid; a sampled one is drawn as scattered points with gaps between them.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Whenever you see the gaps, that is the honest picture of what testing alone can show.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: It does not establish how any particular company runs its flow. Those details, including the tools chosen, the size of teams and the cost of a design, are mostly proprietary, and published estimates vary so widely that this script states none of them.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: It also does not establish that any shipped chip is free of bugs.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Verification proves properties inside models, and the models themselves are assumptions about how silicon behaves. The published errata are the reminder of where that gap shows.

heading: Closing
narration: So a microchip is designed the way a careful argument is written: stated in a precise language, translated step by step, and checked at each step against something it must agree with.

heading: Closing
narration: The chip you are holding is the last link in that chain.

heading: Closing
narration: The evidence that it works is not one test, but the agreement of all of them.
